How I Keep the Mac and Windows Versions of My App in Sync When AI Writes the Code: One Home for the Specs

Hi, I’m Shu.

I’m building Memotori, an on-device transcription and summary app, for both Mac and Windows. Almost all of the code is written by AI (Claude).

I just shipped 1.1.0 on both platforms. It’s the first release where the Mac and Windows versions got the same features, with the same wording.

What made that possible wasn’t how the code was written. It was giving the specs a single home. In this post I’ll show how that works, with the real files. I hope it helps anyone building an app for more than one OS with AI.

The problem: two versions slowly drifting apart

The Mac version (Swift) and the Windows version (C#) live in separate repositories. At first, I asked the AI to “add this feature” in each repository separately.

Little by little, they drifted:

  • The same feature had different button labels on each platform
  • A bug fixed on one side was still there on the other
  • I forgot that some features existed on only one side

The AI only knows the repository it has open. Whatever we decided for the other version, it only knows if I explain it every time. And I forget to explain.

What I did: a spec folder that sits outside both versions

I created a shared working folder above the two repositories, with a spec/ folder for specs that apply to both.

Memotori/
├── Memotori-mac/   ← Mac repository
├── Memotori-win/   ← Windows repository
├── spec/           ← specs shared by both versions
├── releases/       ← release notes shared by both
└── CLAUDE.md       ← working rules for the AI

The AI works in this folder, so it sees both codebases and the specs at once.

Inside spec/ there are four parts:

  • features/ — the current spec, one file per feature
  • changes/ — numbered change proposals (0001, 0002…), with the background and what changes
  • differences.md — what we deliberately don’t align, or haven’t aligned yet
  • ideas.md — ideas that aren’t specs yet

The key is separating “the current spec” from “change proposals.” I want to keep each proposal with the discussion behind it. But when I just want to know how things work today, rereading ten proposals is painful. So once a proposal ships on both platforms, I rewrite the current spec in features/.

The flow for adding a feature

The working rules live in CLAUDE.md, which the AI reads every time. Adding a feature goes like this:

  1. Write the spec first. Copy the template into changes/, give it a number, and add a row to the status table.
  2. Ship it on both versions. If we stop with only one side done, say so in the status table and the spec.
  3. One PR per platform. Each PR mentions the spec number (e.g. spec 0008).
  4. After merging, update the spec’s status and the table, and rewrite the current spec in features/.

The spec template is just this:

# NNNN Feature name
| Platform | Status | PR |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | Not started | — |
| Windows | Not started | — |
## Background       why we're adding it
## Spec             what it does, and how it behaves
## Wording          on-screen text in Japanese and English
## Settings         what each setting is called on Mac and on Windows
## Differences      what can't be aligned, and why

What worked 1: write the UI text in the spec, in both languages

This helped the most. Button labels and messages go into the spec’s “Wording” table, in both Japanese and English. The implementation uses that text as-is.

That way, the AI doesn’t invent wording on the spot, and the Mac and Windows button labels stopped drifting.

Some words do change by OS, though. Where the Mac says “this Mac,” Windows says “this PC.” So I made one substitution table:

  • this PC → this Mac
  • File Explorer → Finder
  • Recycle Bin → Trash

Specs are written with the Windows words, and the Mac version substitutes them using this table.

What worked 2: say clearly when something is one-sided

The status table records, for every feature, whether it’s “Not started / In progress / Done / Won’t do” on Mac and on Windows.

“Won’t do” matters too. For example, one bug fix (spec 0016) was marked “Won’t do (the check doesn’t exist there)” for Windows, because Windows never had that check in the first place. Writing down the reason means that six months later, I won’t wonder, “Did we forget this on Windows?”

The same goes for bug fixes. When we fix something on one side, we check whether the other side has the same bug. That’s also a rule in CLAUDE.md.

What worked 3: keep the release notes in the shared folder too

releases/1.1.0.md lists the specs included in the release, plus the “What’s New” text for the stores in Japanese and English. Both stores use exactly the same text.

What didn’t work

To be honest, there are still holes.

Forgetting to update the status. The headline feature of 1.1.0, to-dos (spec 0008), is on both platforms and already shipped. But when I looked back while writing this post, the status table still said “Not started.” Neither I nor the AI had done the “update the status” step after merging. Even with a system in place, that last rewrite is easy to miss. Now I cross-check the status table whenever I write the release notes.

Writing specs takes effort. Writing a spec even for small changes felt like a chore at first. But when I talk it through with the AI at the spec stage, the “what happens in this case?” questions come up early. There’s less rework after implementation, so overall I think it’s faster.

Memotori 1.1.0, built this way

Finally, let me introduce Memotori 1.1.0, built with this process. Ten specs, 0004 through 0013, shipped on both Mac and Windows.

You can now pull to-dos out of your meetings and check them off as you go. Suggested to-dos aren’t added to your list automatically; you review them first.

Press “Extract To-dos” on a transcript and suggestions appear on the right. Phrases like “by next Friday” become suggested due dates. (The screenshot shows the Japanese UI.)

Added to-dos go into one list across all your meetings, sorted by due date.

Other changes in this release:

  • Summaries and to-dos now live in a pane on the right, with copy, delete, and stop in its header.
  • Rename recordings in your history, and keep the meeting date and time separately.
  • Choose the microphone and language right on the recording screen. Speakers are now identified after you stop recording.
  • If your selected microphone can’t be found, you can pick another one and start recording.

Transcription and summaries run entirely on your device. Your audio and transcripts never leave it.

  • Mac (App Store): apps.apple.com/app/memotori/id6814051112
  • Windows (Microsoft Store): apps.microsoft.com/detail/9N7KPTFRFX2M
  • Questions, bug reports, and requests on Discord: discord.gg/rrH2DnJJjr

  • I Built an On-Device Transcription App for Mac and Windows with AI — Without Touching the Code
  • One Week of Promoting My Indie App: The Real Numbers, and Two Traps I Fell Into

Thanks for reading.

medium.resumo: 2,539 exposed credentials came from a settings file, not AI-generated code. Here is what actually happened and what to check.
medium.conteudo_html:
2,539 exposed credentials came from a settings file, not AI-generated code. Here is what actually happened and what to check.

This story was written with AI assistance.

When developers talk about the security risks in AI coding tools, the conversation goes predictable places. The AI might write code with an injection vulnerability. It might hallucinate an API and produce auth logic that looks right but leaks data. It might miss an edge case a human reviewer would catch. These are real concerns. They are not where the first real incident happened at scale.

Security researchers at Apiiro found 2,539 real secrets exposed in 1,994 public GitHub repositories: database passwords, AWS credentials, SSH keys, GitHub tokens, npm tokens. Most of them came from one file: .claude/settings.local.json.

This is what Claude Code writes when you click "Yes, and don't ask again."

How the File Gets Created

Claude Code asks for permission before it runs commands that touch your system: running shell scripts, writing to certain paths, calling external services. When you approve one of those requests and choose "don't ask again," Claude Code stores that approval in .claude/settings.local.json as a persistent allow rule.

The design intent is reasonable. Approving the same low-risk command twenty times per session is friction with no benefit. So the tool creates a record.

The problem is what that record can contain. If the command you approved included a secret, a database connection string with a password, an API key passed as a flag, an environment variable with a credential, that command gets written to the file verbatim. The file was not added to .gitignore by default. So developers committed it.

Apiiro found .claude/settings.local.json in 103,617 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 1,994 had real credentials inside them. The breakdown: 379 database passwords, 43 SSH logins for live servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS access keys. Expanding the scan to git history, shared settings files and agent transcripts brought the total to 2,539 distinct secrets across 63 organisations.

Anthropics confirmed the finding and announced a fix that adds the file to .gitignore for new projects going forward. The existing 1,994 repositories are not retroactively protected.

The AI Did Not Do This

This is the part worth sitting with. The AI did not hallucinate a password. It did not write insecure code. It did not make a mistake in any conventional sense.

It stored a permission you granted, in a file, in a directory it created, without defaulting to gitignore protection for that directory. The failure mode is a missing default, not a model failure.

That matters because it changes what you should actually be auditing.

The intuitive response to a headline about AI coding tools exposing thousands of secrets is to review the code the AI generated. But in this case, reviewing every AI-written function in every file would have found nothing. The issue was not in the application code. It was in the tool's own configuration artifacts, a layer most developers do not think to include in a security review.

Why This Pattern Keeps Appearing

This is not the first time a developer tool's configuration file has ended up on GitHub full of credentials. The .env file has been doing this for years. The AWS credentials file at ~/.aws/credentials gets committed regularly. SSH private keys surface in public repos on a predictable schedule.

The pattern is consistent: a tool creates a file for convenience or configuration, the file ends up containing something sensitive, and the developer commits it because nothing about the workflow flagged it as different from any other file.

AI coding tools make this pattern easier to trigger, for one specific reason: speed. When you are working with an agent running dozens of actions per session, you approve things faster. The intent behind "don't ask again" is right, stop interrupting developers for low-risk repeated operations. The side effect is that the approval loop runs faster than your mental model of what is being approved.

A security-conscious developer reviewing traditional code reads what they wrote. Reviewing an AI-assisted session means reading what the AI wrote and also checking what the AI was permitted to do, in what files, with what contents. That second part is new, and most developers have not built the habit yet.

What to Check Right Now

If you use Claude Code on any project that touches real credentials, there are four things worth doing:

  • Check whether .claude/settings.local.json is in your .gitignore. If the latest version of Claude Code has not added it automatically, add it manually.
  • Search your git history for the file by running: git log --all --full-history -- ".claude/settings.local.json". This shows whether the file was ever committed, even if it no longer appears in the current working tree.
  • Rotate any credential that might have appeared in a command you approved in a session on that project. If you approved a database migration command that included a connection string, treat that credential as compromised regardless of whether the file appears in a public scan.
  • Review what else is in your .claude directory. Even without credentials, files that record your command history and permissions can reveal internal infrastructure patterns to anyone who can read them.

This applies to any project where you used Claude Code before the gitignore fix was in place. Projects created after the fix gets shipped will have the protection automatically.

The Actual Shape of AI Tool Risk

The gap between where people focus security attention and where failures actually happen is wide.

The dominant fear with AI coding tools is the code they produce: subtle logic errors, hallucinated functions, security bugs woven into application code. Those risks are real and worth auditing. But the first significant incident at scale was not about any of those things. It was about a configuration file that contained what it contained because of a reasonable convenience feature and a missing default.

That changes what a thorough security review looks like for AI-assisted projects. Traditional code review catches problems in source files. AI tool security also requires reviewing what the tool writes outside the source tree: configuration files, permission records, session artifacts. These files are created by the tool itself, not the developer, which makes them easy to overlook.

Prompting Claude Code differently would not have prevented this. Using it less would not have made it worse. The fix is a missing .gitignore entry, and Anthropic has announced one.

The shape of AI tool risk is different from what most developers have been auditing. The place to start is running git log --all --full-history -- ".claude/settings.local.json" on every project where you have used Claude Code with real credentials. That search takes ten seconds and tells you exactly whether you are exposed.

medium.titulo: Build Your Own API Gateway - The Backend Project Nobody Tells You About
medium.resumo: Here’s an idea for your next real-world, resume-worthy backend project - your own API Gateway.
medium.conteudo_html:
Here’s an idea for your next real-world, resume-worthy backend project - your own API Gateway.

It’s the front door every big company puts in front of its APIs. Build one, and you’ll finally understand auth, rate limiting, caching, and failure handling - the stuff tutorials skip.

The Problem to Solve

Every serious product runs on many APIs. Users, payments, orders, notifications - often built by different teams, sometimes in different languages.

Without a front door, every service has to re-implement the same things:

  • Checking who is calling (auth).
  • Stopping one client from flooding the system (rate limiting).
  • Logging every request.
  • Handling timeouts, CORS, versioning, and errors the same way everywhere.

That’s duplicated, inconsistent, and a security risk - one team forgets one check, and that’s your breach.

Big companies solve this with an API Gateway - a single entry point in front of all their services. You’ve used products built on Azure API Management, AWS API Gateway, and Kong without ever seeing them.

I work with Azure API Management in my internship, and honestly - the fastest way to understand what it’s doing is to build a mini version yourself.

Your Project Goal

Build a lightweight API gateway that sits in front of 2–3 small services and can:

  • Route requests by path: /users/* → user service, /orders/* → order service.
  • Authenticate every request with API keys or JWT - before it ever reaches a service.
  • Rate limit per client - e.g. 100 requests/minute, then return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.
  • Cache safe GET responses for a few seconds to take load off your backends.
  • Time out slow services - never let one slow backend freeze the whole gateway.
  • Log every request: client, route, status code, latency, and a request ID.
  • Show a small dashboard: requests per minute, error rate, slowest routes, top clients.

How It Works - One Request, Start to Finish

  1. A client sends a request with its API key or JWT.
  2. Auth: the gateway verifies the key (cached in Redis) and finds the client’s plan. Invalid? 401 - done.
  3. Rate limit: check the client’s counter. Over the limit? 429 immediately - the backend is never touched.
  4. Cache: for GET requests, look up the cache. Hit? Return instantly.
  5. Route: forward to the right service with a timeout (say 3 seconds) and a request ID header for tracing. Too slow? 504 Gateway Timeout instead of hanging forever.
  6. Log: record status and latency, cache the response if allowed, and send it back.
  7. The dashboard reads the logs and shows what’s happening - live.

Notice the order: the cheapest checks run first. Rejecting a bad request at step 2 or 3 costs microseconds; letting it reach your database costs real money.

Why This Project is Worth Building

  • Real-world use case: Every large system has a gateway. This is exactly what production backends look like.
  • Interview gold: “Design a rate limiter” and “Design an API gateway” are classic system design questions - and you’ll have actually built both.
  • The “boring” parts that matter: Security, reliability, and observability - the skills that separate developers from engineers.
  • Startup potential: A simple, cheap gateway for small teams and indie developers is a real product idea.

Suggested Tech Stack

Gateway

  • Node.js + Express (or Fastify / NestJS) - with http-proxy-middleware to forward requests.

Rate Limiting & Caching

  • Redis - fast counters that expire on their own. Start with INCR + EXPIRE (fixed window), then try sorted sets for a sliding window.

Auth

  • JWT verification and hashed API keys (never store raw keys - treat them like passwords).

Database

  • PostgreSQL - API keys, plans, and request logs.

Dashboard

  • React or Next.js with any chart library.

Infra

  • Docker Compose to run the gateway, services, and Redis together locally.
  • Railway / Render to host it.

Build It in 4 Weeks

Week 1 - Proxy & routing

  • Two dummy services + a gateway that forwards /users/* and /orders/*.
  • Add timeouts and a request ID from day one.

Week 2 - Auth & rate limiting

  • API keys (hashed) and JWT verification.
  • A Redis rate limiter that returns 429 with Retry-After.

Week 3 - Caching & logging

  • Cache safe GETs with a short TTL.
  • Log every request to PostgreSQL.

Week 4 - Dashboard & load test

  • A small dashboard for traffic, errors, and latency.
  • Load-test it and fix whatever breaks first.

Mistakes Most People Make

  • Caching per route, not per user. If /orders is cached without the client ID in the cache key, user A can see user B's orders. Always include who's asking - or only cache truly public data.
  • No timeouts. One slow service and every gateway worker sits waiting. Set a timeout on every upstream call.
  • Rate limiting by IP only. Behind a load balancer, everyone can look like the same IP - and X-Forwarded-For is easy to fake. Rate limit by API key or user, and only trust forwarded headers from your own proxy.
  • Storing raw API keys. Store a hash, show the key once at creation.
  • Running a single copy. Your gateway is now the front door - if it goes down, everything goes down.

Design for Scale

Keep the gateway stateless - all shared state (rate-limit counters, cache) lives in Redis. Then you can run two or more copies behind a load balancer: if one crashes, the other keeps serving, and adding capacity is just adding another copy.

Extra Features to Try

  • Plans: Free = 100 requests/day, Pro = 10,000 - just like real API products.
  • Circuit breaker: if a service keeps failing, stop sending it traffic for 30 seconds instead of making things worse.
  • API versioning: route /v1 and /v2 to different services.
  • Request transformation: strip internal headers, rename fields.
  • Developer portal: let users sign up and generate their own API keys.

Why You Should Try This Project

This isn’t another CRUD app. It pushes you to:

  • Think about every request, not just the happy path.
  • Handle failure - slow services, abusive clients, expired tokens.
  • Design for scale - stateless services, shared state, no single point of failure.
  • Understand tools like Azure API Management or AWS API Gateway from the inside out - so when you use them at work, you know exactly what they’re doing.

If you want to stand out in backend interviews - this, is it.

Pro Tip: Load-test your gateway with k6 or autocannon. Post a screenshot of it calmly returning 429s under a flood of requests on LinkedIn - that one image says more than a whole “skills” section.

In the next post, I’ll break down rate limiting algorithms - fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket - with simple diagrams.

medium.titulo: Nuxt 4.6 Vapor Interop: Adopting Vapor Mode One Page at a Time
medium.resumo: A beginner-friendly, hands-on guide to Vue’s Virtual-DOM-free rendering mode inside a real Nuxt app, without rewriting everything at once.
medium.conteudo_html:
A beginner-friendly, hands-on guide to Vue’s Virtual-DOM-free rendering mode inside a real Nuxt app, without rewriting everything at once.

Nuxt 4.6 lets you switch a single page or component to Vue’s new Vapor Mode by adding one word to its <script setup> tag. The rest of your app keeps running exactly as before. That is what "interop mode" means, and it is the safest way to try the biggest change to Vue's rendering engine since Vue 3 itself.

Nuxt 4.6 shipped on October 5, 2026, with more than 420 commits. It brought a lot: nuxt/server, rebuilt typed $fetch, sealed-cookie sessions, a new CLI. Hidden in that list is a feature that changes how your components actually paint pixels: Vue Vapor support.

Most articles about Vapor show a counter, quote a benchmark and stop. This one goes further. By the end you will understand:

  • what the Virtual DOM does and why Vapor can skip it
  • what “interop mode” means and why Nuxt keeps your app root on the Virtual DOM
  • how to enable Vapor in Nuxt 4.6, step by step, with every line of code explained
  • how to convert one real, data-heavy page to Vapor
  • the “boundary rule” that decides whether mixing modes helps or hurts
  • every known limitation, with a working fix for each
  • a page-by-page playbook to adopt Vapor safely, measure it, and roll back if needed

No prior Vapor knowledge is needed. If you know what a .vue file and ref() are, you are ready.

A quick honesty note before we start. Vapor depends on Vue 3.6, which is still a release candidate at the time of writing. Treat everything here as something to evaluate, not something to ship to production tomorrow. I’ll point out exactly where the sharp edges are.

Part 1: A quick refresher on how Vue renders today

To understand why Vapor is a big deal, you first need to know what it replaces: the Virtual DOM (VDOM).

The real DOM is slow to touch

The browser’s DOM is the live tree of elements you see on screen. Reading and writing it is relatively expensive: every change can trigger style recalculation, layout and paint. Early JavaScript apps updated the DOM by hand, and it was easy to make too many changes or forget one.

The Virtual DOM idea

Frameworks like Vue and React introduced a middle layer. Instead of touching the DOM directly, your component describes what the UI should look like as plain JavaScript objects. These objects are called VNodes (virtual nodes), and the whole set of them is the Virtual DOM tree.

When your data changes, the framework:

  1. Runs your component’s render function again.
  2. Builds a brand-new VNode tree.
  3. Compares (“diffs”) the new tree against the previous one.
  4. Applies only the differences to the real DOM (“patching”).

Here is a tiny component you have probably written a hundred times:

<!-- app/components/Counter.vue (classic, Virtual DOM) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
const count = ref(0)
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">
    count is {{ count }}
  </button>
</template>

What is happening here, line by line:

  • <script setup lang="ts"> is the Composition API shorthand. Everything declared inside is available to the template. lang="ts" just means TypeScript.
  • const count = ref(0) creates a reactive value. Vue tracks who reads count, so it knows what to update when it changes. In Nuxt, ref is auto-imported, so there is no import line.
  • @click="count++" is shorthand for v-on:click. Clicking increments the value.
  • {{ count }} prints the current value as text.

Behind the scenes, Vue compiles the <template> into a render function. Each time count changes, that function runs again and produces fresh VNodes. Vue then diffs them and updates the button's text.

Why the Virtual DOM was a good trade-off

The VDOM made UI code declarative: you describe the result, and the framework works out the steps. It also made features like render functions, JSX and component libraries that inspect VNodes possible.

The cost is overhead. Even with Vue 3’s clever compiler optimizations (patch flags and block trees that skip static parts), every update still re-runs the render function and allocates new VNode objects, then compares them. For most screens this is fast enough. For big tables, dashboards, live feeds and long lists, that overhead adds up in CPU time, memory and the amount of runtime code shipped to the browser.

That overhead is exactly what Vapor removes.

Part 2: What Vapor Mode actually is

Vapor Mode is a second way to compile the same .vue file. Instead of turning your template into a render function that produces VNodes, the compiler turns it into code that creates real DOM nodes once and then updates them directly when data changes.

The Vue core team describes it as a new compilation mode for Single-File Components that aims to reduce baseline bundle size and improve performance. They also report that Vapor reaches the same performance level as Solid and Svelte 5 in the community js-framework-benchmark.

The key insight: the compiler already knows what can change

Look at the counter template again. The compiler can see, at build time, that:

  • the <button> element never changes its tag or structure
  • the click listener never changes
  • only one thing is dynamic: the text that shows count

With the Virtual DOM, Vue still re-runs the whole render function at runtime to rediscover this. Vapor uses the knowledge directly. It generates code that says, in effect, “when count changes, set the text of this node". There is nothing to diff, because nothing else could have changed.

This works because of Vue’s fine-grained reactivity. Every ref already tracks exactly which effects read it. Vapor wires each dynamic spot in the template to its own tiny effect. When count changes, only that effect re-runs.

What the compiler produces

You never write the compiled output yourself, but seeing a simplified version helps the idea click.

Here is the same idea as code you can read (simplified pseudo-code, not the exact output of Vue’s compiler):

// Classic (Virtual DOM): runs on EVERY update
function render() {
  return h('button', { onClick: () => count.value++ },
    `count is ${count.value}`)
}

// Vapor: setup runs ONCE, then only the effect re-runs
const tmpl = template('<button> </button>')   // static HTML, parsed once
function setup() {
  const button = tmpl()                       // clone real DOM nodes
  delegate(button, 'click', () => count.value++)
  renderEffect(() => {
    setText(button.firstChild, `count is ${count.value}`)
  })
  return button
}

How to read this comparison:

  • In the classic version, render() is called again after every click. Each call allocates a new VNode object for the button and a new string. Vue then compares the old and new VNodes before touching the DOM.
  • In the Vapor version, template() turns the static HTML into DOM nodes once. Cloning ready-made nodes is very cheap for the browser.
  • delegate(...) registers the click handler. We will see later why "delegate" matters (it is one of the gotchas).
  • renderEffect(...) is the heart of Vapor. It is a reactive effect that reads count. When count changes, Vue re-runs only this function, which sets one text node. No VNodes, no diff.

What you get, and what you give up

Benefits Vapor is designed for:

  • Less work per update: CPU time scales with what changed, not with the size of the component’s render output.
  • Less memory: no VNode trees kept around for comparison.
  • Smaller baseline bundle, but only for apps that are entirely Vapor (more on this soon, because it matters a lot for Nuxt).

The trade-off: Vapor supports a subset of Vue. Anything that depends on VNodes or on the component instance proxy (this, $el, $refs and friends) is not available. In practice that means <script setup> or template-only components, with no Options API. Part 8 lists every limitation with a fix.

How you opt in

At the Vue level, you mark a component with the vapor attribute. Vue 3.6 accepts three equivalent forms:

<!-- 1. The most common form -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
// ...
</script>

<!-- 2. Shorthand: <script vapor> means <script setup vapor> -->
<script vapor lang="ts">
// ...
</script>

<!-- 3. On the template: compiles the whole SFC in Vapor mode -->
<template vapor>
  <!-- ... -->
</template>

That one attribute is the whole opt-in. You do not change your template syntax, your refs or your computeds. The difference is entirely in what the compiler emits.

Part 3: “Interop mode” and why Nuxt keeps the root on the Virtual DOM

Vue 3.6 gives you two ways to run Vapor components.

Option A: a pure Vapor app. Every component is Vapor, and the app is created with createVaporApp(). The Virtual DOM runtime is never loaded, which is where the big bundle-size savings come from.

// A pure Vapor app (plain Vue, not Nuxt)
import { createVaporApp } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'

createVaporApp(App).mount('#app')

Option B: interop. You keep a normal Virtual DOM app created with createApp(), and install vaporInteropPlugin. Now Vapor and classic components can be nested inside each other.

// A classic app that can host Vapor components (plain Vue, not Nuxt)
import { createApp, vaporInteropPlugin } from 'vue'
import App from './App.vue'

createApp(App)
  .use(vaporInteropPlugin) // the bridge between the two runtimes
  .mount('#app')

Nuxt 4.6 uses Option B. When you turn on vue.vapor, Nuxt installs vaporInteropPlugin for you. Nuxt's application root and its own internals stay on the Virtual DOM, and so does every component you haven't marked. You then opt individual pages or components into Vapor.

Why not a fully Vapor Nuxt app?

Nuxt is built from a lot of Virtual DOM machinery: <NuxtLayout>, <NuxtPage>, <ClientOnly>, islands, head management, plus every module in the ecosystem. Many of these inspect slots or VNodes, which Vapor intentionally does not have. Nuxt's docs say plainly that full Vapor apps are not supported yet and the app root stays VDOM, though they may support it later.

So interop is not a compromise you should feel bad about. It is the only practical way to bring Vapor into a framework of Nuxt’s size, and it is exactly what makes page-by-page adoption possible.

The honest trade-off: interop can mean more JavaScript, not less

This is the part most “Vapor is faster!” posts skip. In interop mode, the browser loads the Virtual DOM runtime (because your app root needs it) and the Vapor runtime (because some components need it). The bundle-size win of a pure Vapor app does not apply.

One real data point: the c15t consent library documents that its Nuxt Vapor test page downloads about 18% more JavaScript than the same app without Vapor.

So in Nuxt 4.6, the reason to adopt Vapor is runtime performance on specific heavy pages, not a smaller download. Keep that framing in mind; it shapes every decision in the playbook later.

What “keeps working” in interop mode

According to the Nuxt 4.6 release notes, routing, useAsyncData, layouts and most built-in components work without changes inside Vapor pages. The Nuxt team taught the auto-import loader, useAsyncData, definePageMeta and slot inspection about Vapor, sent fixes upstream to Vue, and added a dedicated Vapor test suite. Most Nuxt composables keep working because they rely on Vue's provide/inject rather than on a component instance.

Part 4: Release status and what you need before starting

Vapor is feature-complete but not yet stable. Vue 3.6 entered the release-candidate phase in July 2026 with the full Vapor feature set, and new RCs have been shipping roughly weekly since. As of mid-October 2026, npm’s latest tag still pointed at the Vue 3.5 line, with 3.6 builds published as release candidates. "Feature-complete" describes scope, not stability, and Vue's own guidance is not to run pre-releases in production.

Nuxt also labels its Vapor support experimental, and says the API may change.

When to try it, and when to wait

  • Try it now in a fresh project, a side branch, an internal tool, or one isolated page where you have measured a rendering bottleneck. The Nuxt team itself recommends starting with a fresh project.
  • Wait before shipping it on a production page that already performs well on Vue 3.5. You would be taking on pre-release risk for no measured gain.

The page-by-page approach in this article is designed so you can do both: experiment for real, while keeping a one-word rollback.

Part 5: Step-by-step setup, your first Vapor page

We will start from zero and end with one Vapor page running next to normal pages.

Step 1: Get a Nuxt 4.6 project

For a brand-new playground (recommended for your first try):

npm create nuxt@latest vapor-lab
cd vapor-lab

For an existing Nuxt 4 project, do this on a new git branch:

git checkout -b try-vapor
npx nuxt upgrade --dedupe

nuxt upgrade --dedupe is the upgrade command the Nuxt team recommends for 4.6. It updates Nuxt and refreshes your lockfile so you don't end up with stale duplicate dependencies.

Step 2: Install a Vue 3.6 release candidate

Nuxt 4.6 still works with Vue 3.5. Vapor needs 3.6, so you install it explicitly:

npm install vue@^3.6.0-rc.6

Your package.json should now contain something like this:

{
  "dependencies": {
    "nuxt": "^4.6.0",
    "vue": "^3.6.0-rc.6"
  }
}

Why the caret matters here: ^3.6.0-rc.6 accepts later release candidates of 3.6.0 and, eventually, the stable 3.6.x releases. So you will pick up interop fixes as they land.

Now make sure only one copy of Vue is installed. Two copies of Vue in one app cause confusing reactivity bugs:

npm ls vue

If you see more than one version, force a single one with npm’s overrides field and reinstall:

{
  "overrides": {
    "vue": "$vue"
  }
}

"$vue" tells npm to reuse the version you declared in dependencies everywhere in the tree. (pnpm and Yarn have equivalent overrides and resolutions settings.)

Step 3: Turn on Vapor support in nuxt.config.ts

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  compatibilityDate: '2026-10-30',
  vue: {
    vapor: true,
  },
})

What this one option does:

  • It tells Nuxt to install Vue’s vaporInteropPlugin on the app, so Vapor and classic components can nest inside each other.
  • It makes Nuxt’s own internals Vapor-aware: auto-imports, useAsyncData, definePageMeta and slot handling.
  • It does not convert anything. Every existing component still compiles exactly as before. Nothing becomes Vapor until you add the vapor attribute to a file.

That last point is what makes this safe. Turning the flag on in an existing app should change nothing visible. If something does break right after enabling it, you have found an interop problem before writing any Vapor code, which is valuable information.

Step 4: Create your first Vapor page

Here is the project structure we are aiming for. Only one file is Vapor:

vapor-lab/
├─ app/
│  ├─ app.vue              ← classic (we leave it alone)
│  ├─ layouts/
│  │  └─ default.vue       ← classic
│  └─ pages/
│     ├─ index.vue         ← classic page
│     └─ vapor-hello.vue   ← our first Vapor page
└─ nuxt.config.ts          ← vue: { vapor: true }

Create app/pages/vapor-hello.vue:

<!-- app/pages/vapor-hello.vue -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
import { getCurrentInstance } from 'vue'

// Nuxt features work as usual inside a Vapor page
definePageMeta({ title: 'Vapor hello' })
useSeoMeta({ title: 'Hello from Vapor' })
const count = ref(0)
const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2)
// Dev-only sanity check: Vapor components have no classic instance
if (import.meta.dev) {
  console.log('[vapor-hello] is Vapor:', getCurrentInstance() === null)
}
</script>
<template>
  <main class="hello">
    <h1>Hello from a Vapor page</h1>
    <button @click="count++">
      count is {{ count }}, doubled is {{ doubled }}
    </button>
    <NuxtLink to="/">Back to a classic page</NuxtLink>
  </main>
</template>
<style scoped>
.hello { display: grid; gap: 1rem; padding: 2rem; }
</style>

Line-by-line explanation:

  • <script setup vapor lang="ts">: the only Vapor-specific thing in the whole file. Remove the word vapor and this is an ordinary Nuxt page again.
  • definePageMeta(...): Nuxt's page-level metadata macro. Nuxt 4.6 taught it about Vapor, so it works here unchanged.
  • useSeoMeta({ title: ... }): sets the document title. In Vapor pages, prefer composables like this over head components such as <Title>, for a reason explained in Part 8.
  • ref, computed: auto-imported by Nuxt, exactly as in classic components. Vapor uses the same reactivity system.
  • The getCurrentInstance() check: Vue's release notes state that getCurrentInstance() returns null in Vapor components. Logging it is a quick way to confirm the file really compiled as Vapor. Wrapping it in import.meta.dev means it is removed from production builds.
  • <NuxtLink>: a classic (VDOM) Nuxt component used inside a Vapor template. This works through the interop plugin. You have just crossed a mode boundary without noticing, which is the point.
  • <style scoped>: styles work the same in both modes.

Step 5: Run it and verify

npx nuxt dev

Open http://localhost:3000/vapor-hello and check three things:

  1. The counter works and the page looks normal.
  2. The browser console prints [vapor-hello] is Vapor: true.
  3. The terminal shows no warning about vue.vapor being disabled. If it does, your installed Vue is too old. Re-check npm ls vue.

Then navigate to / and back. Routing between a classic page and a Vapor page should feel identical. Congratulations: you are running a mixed-mode Nuxt app.

Part 6: A realistic example, converting a heavy catalog page

A counter proves the setup works. It does not show where Vapor earns its keep. So let’s build the kind of page Vapor is designed for: a product catalog with 2,000 rows, live search, sorting and an “add to cart” toggle on every row.

We need four files:

shared/types/product.ts        ← one shared type
server/api/products.get.ts     ← fake data API
app/components/ProductRow.vue  ← Vapor child (one row)
app/pages/catalog.vue          ← Vapor page (owns the list)

File 1: a shared type

// shared/types/product.ts
export interface Product {
  id: number
  name: string
  category: string
  price: number
  stock: number
}

Nuxt 4’s shared/ folder is visible to both the server and the app, so one interface describes the data everywhere.

File 2: the data API

// server/api/products.get.ts
import { defineEventHandler } from 'nuxt/server'
import type { Product } from '~~/shared/types/product'

const categories = ['Books', 'Games', 'Garden', 'Kitchen', 'Toys']
// 2,000 fake products, generated once when the server starts
const products: Product[] = Array.from({ length: 2000 }, (_, i) => ({
  id: i + 1,
  name: `Product ${String(i + 1).padStart(4, '0')}`,
  category: categories[i % categories.length]!,
  price: 5 + ((i * 37) % 200),
  stock: (i * 13) % 50,
}))
export default defineEventHandler(() => products)

What to notice:

  • import { defineEventHandler } from 'nuxt/server' uses the new server import surface that also shipped in Nuxt 4.6. It is unrelated to Vapor, but it is the forward-compatible way to write handlers that will run unchanged on Nuxt 5.
  • The data is deterministic (no Math.random()), so the server-rendered HTML and the browser render agree. That avoids hydration mismatches, which are confusing to debug in any mode.
  • ~~ is Nuxt's alias for the project root.

File 3: one row, as a Vapor component

<!-- app/components/ProductRow.vue -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
import type { Product } from '~~/shared/types/product'

const props = defineProps<{
  product: Product
  inCart: boolean
}>()
const emit = defineEmits<{
  toggle: [id: number]
}>()
const priceLabel = computed(() => `$${props.product.price.toFixed(2)}`)
const lowStock = computed(() => props.product.stock < 5)
</script>
<template>
  <li class="row" :class="{ 'row--low': lowStock }">
    <span class="name">{{ product.name }}</span>
    <span class="category">{{ product.category }}</span>
    <span class="price">{{ priceLabel }}</span>
    <button type="button" @click="emit('toggle', product.id)">
      {{ inCart ? 'Remove' : 'Add to cart' }}
    </button>
  </li>
</template>

How this works in Vapor:

  • defineProps and defineEmits are the normal <script setup> macros. They work the same in Vapor.
  • defineEmits<{ toggle: [id: number] }>() is the typed "named tuple" syntax: the toggle event carries one argument, a number.
  • In the template, the compiler finds five dynamic spots: the row--low class, the name, the category, the price label and the button text. Each one gets its own small render effect.
  • When the user adds this product to the cart, only inCart changes for this row. So only one effect runs: the one that sets the button's text. The other 1,999 rows do no work at all.

File 4: the page that owns the list

<!-- app/pages/catalog.vue -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
// 1. Nuxt composables first: before any `await`
const route = useRoute()
const router = useRouter()

// 2. Start the data request, but don't await it yet
const asyncProducts = useAsyncData(
  'catalog-products',
  () => $fetch('/api/products'),
  { default: () => [] },
)
const products = asyncProducts.data
const status = asyncProducts.status
// 3. Local UI state, seeded from the URL (?q=...)
const search = ref(String(route.query.q ?? ''))
const sortBy = ref<'name' | 'price'>('name')
const cart = ref(new Set<number>())
// 4. Derived state: recomputed only when its inputs change
const visible = computed(() => {
  const q = search.value.trim().toLowerCase()
  const list = q
    ? products.value.filter(p => p.name.toLowerCase().includes(q))
    : products.value
  return [...list].sort((a, b) =>
    sortBy.value === 'price' ? a.price - b.price : a.name.localeCompare(b.name),
  )
})
// 5. Keep the URL in sync so searches are shareable
watch(search, (q) => {
  router.replace({ query: { ...route.query, q: q || undefined } })
})
function toggleCart(id: number) {
  if (cart.value.has(id)) cart.value.delete(id)
  else cart.value.add(id)
}
useSeoMeta({ title: 'Catalog' })
// 6. The ONE await, at the very end
await asyncProducts
</script>
<template>
  <section class="catalog">
    <header class="toolbar">
      <input v-model="search" type="search" placeholder="Search 2,000 products">
      <select v-model="sortBy">
        <option value="name">Sort by name</option>
        <option value="price">Sort by price</option>
      </select>
      <span>{{ visible.length }} shown · {{ cart.size }} in cart</span>
    </header>
    <p v-if="status === 'pending'">Loading products…</p>
    <ul v-else class="list">
      <ProductRow
        v-for="product in visible"
        :key="product.id"
        :product="product"
        :in-cart="cart.has(product.id)"
        @toggle="toggleCart"
      />
    </ul>
  </section>
</template>

Walking through the page

Section 1: composables before await. useRoute() and useRouter() need Nuxt's context. In a classic <script setup>, Vue's compiler quietly restores that context after each await. The Nuxt docs warn that in a Vapor <script setup>, Nuxt composables called after an await may lose their context. The simplest habit that avoids the problem entirely: call every composable at the top.

Section 2: start the request, await later. useAsyncData returns an object that is also a promise. We keep the object, read data and status from it immediately, and only await it at the end (section 6). The default: () => [] option means products.value is always an array, so the computed below never has to handle null.

Section 3: plain reactive state. ref(new Set<number>()) works because Vue's reactivity tracks Set operations like .add(), .delete() and .has().

Section 4: the computed. visible re-runs only when search, sortBy or products change. Typing in the search box updates visible, and Vapor's v-for then adds, moves or removes row components by their :key.

Section 5: watch. Mirrors the search text into the URL with router.replace, so reloading or sharing the link keeps the search. q || undefined removes the parameter when the box is empty.

Section 6: the single await. Awaiting at the end means the server waits for the data before rendering HTML, which is what you want for SEO. Because everything else was set up before it, there is nothing left that could lose context.

The template: v-model, v-if/v-else, v-for with :key, props and events all look exactly like classic Vue. The page passes toggleCart down, the row emits toggle with its id, and the page updates the Set.

Why this page benefits from Vapor

Walk through what happens when a user clicks “Add to cart” on one row.

With the Virtual DOM, cart changes and the page's render function runs again. It builds a new list of 2,000 row VNodes. Vue compares each row's props with the previous ones. Vue 3 is smart about it and only re-renders the one row whose inCart prop changed, but it still had to create and compare the VNodes for the whole list.

With Vapor, there is no page render function to re-run. Each row’s :in-cart binding is its own effect that depends on cart. When the Set changes, Vue re-checks those bindings and only one row's button text is updated. The work is tied to the data, not to the length of the template.

This is the shape of page where Vapor helps: large lists, frequent small updates, and interactions that should feel instant. A mostly static marketing page with a contact form is not that shape, and would gain little.

What converting it actually cost

If you already had this page as classic Vue, the whole conversion was two words:

- <script setup lang="ts">
+ <script setup vapor lang="ts">

…in catalog.vue and in ProductRow.vue, plus moving composables above the await. That is what "one page at a time" means in practice.

Part 7: The boundary rule, where Virtual DOM and Vapor meet

Every time a classic component renders a Vapor component (or the other way round), the interop layer has to translate between two different worlds: props, events and slots in VNode form on one side, and real DOM blocks with render effects on the other. That translation is a mode crossing. It works, but it is not free.

The Vue team’s advice in the 3.6 release notes is clear: keep distinct regions of your app in one mode or the other, and avoid mixed nesting as much as possible. In practice that becomes one rule:

Put the boundary above the repeated part, never inside it.

The anti-pattern

<!-- app/components/ProductList.vue: classic (no vapor attribute) -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import type { Product } from '~~/shared/types/product'
defineProps<{ products: Product[] }>()
</script>

<template>
  <ul>
    <!-- ProductRow is Vapor: one crossing PER ROW -->
    <ProductRow v-for="p in products" :key="p.id" :product="p" :in-cart="false" />
  </ul>
</template>

Here the list is classic and each row is Vapor. With 500 products, the interop layer works 500 times on every list render. You could even end up slower than an all-classic list, because you pay Vapor’s setup cost plus interop translation for every row, while the list itself still re-renders through the Virtual DOM.

The fix

Make the component that owns the loop Vapor too (or, as in Part 6, the page itself):

<!-- app/components/ProductList.vue -->
- <script setup lang="ts">
+ <script setup vapor lang="ts">

Now there is one crossing (where the classic parent renders ProductList), and everything below it, all 500 rows, is pure Vapor.

The same rule for UI-library components

The sneakier version of this problem is a component library. Suppose each row shows a badge from a VDOM-based UI kit:

<!-- inside a Vapor ProductRow -->
<UiBadge :color="lowStock ? 'red' : 'gray'">{{ product.category }}</UiBadge>

That is a Vapor-to-VDOM crossing inside every row, with a slot passing across it. Slots are where interop is roughest: Vue’s notes say interop covers standard props, events and slots, but not every edge case, and they specifically mention rough edges with VDOM component libraries. For example, Nuxt UI has a tracking issue for Vapor support that was first filed after slot-related runtime errors inside Vapor parents.

You have three options, from best to worst:

  1. Use plain markup inside hot loops. A styled <span class="badge"> costs nothing and has no boundary.
  2. Write a tiny Vapor version of the component for use inside Vapor regions.
  3. Keep the row classic if it truly needs the library component, and accept that this list is not a good Vapor candidate yet.

Outside loops, a single library component (a modal, a date picker in the header) inside a Vapor page is usually fine. One crossing is cheap. Five hundred are not.

A quick boundary checklist

  • Every v-for in a Vapor region renders Vapor children (or plain elements).
  • Library components inside Vapor regions sit outside loops, or have been tested inside them.
  • Slots passed across a boundary are passed explicitly in the template (never computed by calling a slot function).
  • Each page is mostly one mode. A page that is half and half is a sign to move the boundary.

Part 8: Known limitations and gotchas, each with a fix

This is the section to bookmark. It combines the limitations listed in the Nuxt docs with the compatibility notes from Vue 3.6, and gives a working fix for each.

Let’s take them one at a time.

1. Call Nuxt composables before the first await

<!-- ✗ Risky in a Vapor component -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
const { data: user } = await useFetch('/api/me')
const route = useRoute()          // may run without Nuxt context
const config = useRuntimeConfig() // same problem
</script>
<!-- ✓ Safe -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
const route = useRoute()
const config = useRuntimeConfig()
const { data: user } = await useFetch('/api/me')
</script>

Why: composables like useRoute() find the current Nuxt app through a hidden "current context". In classic <script setup>, Vue's compiler restores that context after each await for you. The Nuxt docs warn that in a Vapor <script setup>, this may not happen. If you need several awaits, start every request first and await them together at the end, as in Part 6.

2. No $el on component refs

In a classic parent, it is common to reach into a child’s root element:

<!-- Parent: works with a classic child, breaks with a Vapor child -->
<script setup lang="ts">
const chart = useTemplateRef('chart')
onMounted(() => {
  resizeObserver.observe(chart.value!.$el) // $el is undefined on a Vapor child
})
</script>

<template>
  <SalesChart ref="chart" />
</template>

Fix: have the Vapor child expose exactly what the parent needs, through a small function:

<!-- app/components/SalesChart.vue -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
const root = useTemplateRef<HTMLDivElement>('root')

defineExpose({
  getRootEl: () => root.value,
})
</script>
<template>
  <div ref="root" class="chart"><!-- … --></div>
</template>
// In the parent
onMounted(() => {
  const el = chart.value?.getRootEl()
  if (el) resizeObserver.observe(el)
})

Why this is better anyway: $el was always an implicit, fragile contract. If the child's root ever changed (a wrapper div, a fragment), the parent silently broke. An exposed function is an explicit API.

3. Head components with Vapor slot content

Components like <Title>, <Style> and <Noscript> read their text children from the slot. They can't read Vapor slot content and will warn. <NuxtIsland> and server components warn too, and <ClientOnly> skips its attribute-forwarding fallthrough.

<!-- ✗ Warns inside a Vapor component -->
<template>
  <Head>
    <Title>{{ product.name }} | Shop</Title>
  </Head>
</template>
<!-- ✓ Use the composable instead -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
const props = defineProps<{ product: Product }>()

useHead({
  title: () => `${props.product.name} | Shop`, // a getter keeps it reactive
})
</script>

The getter () => ... matters: it lets the title update when the product changes.

4. No Options API

Vapor only compiles <script setup> and template-only components. If an old page uses defineNuxtComponent with asyncData, rewrite it before adding vapor:

// ✗ Before: Options API (cannot be Vapor)
export default defineNuxtComponent({
  async asyncData() {
    return { posts: await $fetch('/api/posts') }
  },
})
<!-- ✓ After: <script setup> (can be Vapor) -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
const { data: posts } = await useAsyncData('posts', () => $fetch('/api/posts'))
</script>

5. No globalProperties: get helpers from useNuxtApp()

Vue’s notes list app.config.globalProperties as unsupported in Vapor, and getCurrentInstance() returns null. In Nuxt, helpers that a plugin provides are often used straight in templates as $name(...), which depends on that global-properties mechanism. Inside Vapor, pull them out in script instead:

// app/plugins/format.ts
export default defineNuxtPlugin(() => ({
  provide: {
    formatPrice: (n: number) => `$${n.toFixed(2)}`,
  },
}))
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
const { $formatPrice } = useNuxtApp() // before any await
</script>

<template>
  <span>{{ $formatPrice(19.5) }}</span>
</template>

Because $formatPrice is now a local variable, the template finds it like any other binding. Libraries that call getCurrentInstance() internally also need checking; they will see null.

6. No v-memo and no per-element lifecycle events

v-memo existed to let you skip Virtual DOM diffing for parts of a big list. Vapor has no diffing to skip, so the directive is unsupported and, more importantly, unnecessary. Just delete it:

- <div v-for="item in list" :key="item.id" v-memo="[item.id === selectedId]">
+ <div v-for="item in list" :key="item.id">

The same goes for per-element lifecycle events like @vue:mounted. Use onMounted in the component, or a template ref.

7. Event delegation and stopPropagation()

This one causes the most confusing bugs, because nothing errors.

For eligible events like click, Vapor doesn't attach a listener to each element. Each element stores its handler, and one listener on document walks the event path and calls the matching handlers. That saves memory and setup time, but it means the click must actually reach document.

If any ancestor calls stopPropagation() (for example a classic modal wrapper with @click.stop), the event stops before it gets there, and your Vapor handler simply never runs.

<!-- A classic parent -->
<div class="modal" @click.stop>
  <SaveButton />   <!-- Vapor child: its @click never fires -->
</div>

Fixes, best first:

  1. Remove the .stop if it isn't really needed. Usually it was added to stop a backdrop click handler; checking event.target === event.currentTarget in that handler does the same job without blocking anything.
  2. If you can’t change the ancestor, bind the handler in a form that skips delegation. The Vue notes list these:
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
function save() { /* … */ }
const evt = 'click'
</script>

<template>
  <!-- each of these attaches the listener directly to the element -->
  <button v-on="{ click: save }">Save</button>
  <button v-bind="{ onClick: save }">Save</button>
  <button @[evt]="save">Save</button>
</template>

8. Never “peek” at a slot by calling it

In classic Vue, some wrapper components call slots.default() to check whether anything was passed. In Vapor, calling a slot function renders it: it creates DOM nodes, registers effects and, during hydration, claims server-rendered HTML.

<!-- ✗ Don't do this in Vapor -->
<script setup vapor lang="ts">
const slots = useSlots()
const isEmpty = !slots.default?.() // renders the slot as a side effect!
</script>
<!-- ✓ Let the template render the slot, with fallback content -->
<template>
  <div class="panel">
    <slot>Nothing to show yet.</slot>
  </div>
</template>

The text between <slot> and </slot> is fallback content: Vue shows it only when the parent passes nothing. If you only need to know whether a slot was provided, checking !!slots.default (without the parentheses) does not call it.

9. Custom directives have a new shape

Classic directives are objects with hooks (mounted, updated, …). A Vapor directive is a single function that receives the element and a getter for the bound value, and may return a cleanup function:

<script setup vapor lang="ts">
// Vapor directive: (element, valueGetter, argument, modifiers) => cleanup?
const vTooltip = (el: Element, value?: () => string) => {
  // watchEffect re-runs whenever the bound value changes,
  // and is stopped automatically when the component unmounts
  watchEffect(() => {
    el.setAttribute('title', value?.() ?? '')
  })
}

const label = ref('Saved 2 minutes ago')
</script>
<template>
  <span v-tooltip="label">Status</span>
</template>

The getter replaces binding.value, and watchEffect replaces the updated hook. Shared directives used in both modes need two versions for now.

10. Smaller notes

  • Keyed onPrehydrate falls back to the unkeyed form in Vapor components and warns in development, because there is no component instance to attach the key to.
  • Render functions and JSX always produce VDOM components. They need interop to appear inside a Vapor region.
  • Tooling: Vue DevTools was built around the Virtual DOM and component instances. Expect a less complete picture of Vapor components there for now, and lean on the browser’s Performance panel for measurements.

Part 9: A page-by-page adoption playbook

You now know what Vapor is, how interop works and where it breaks. Here is how to roll it into a real app without gambling: one page at a time, measuring at every step, with a rollback that is literally one word.

Phase 0: Prepare

On a branch, upgrade to Nuxt 4.6, install the Vue 3.6 RC, and turn on vue.vapor: true (Part 5). Do not add any vapor attributes yet.

Gate: the build passes, your tests pass and the app behaves exactly as before. This proves the interop plugin itself is harmless in your app.

Phase 1: Baseline

Pick 2 or 3 candidate pages: the ones that feel sluggish when users interact with them. Record numbers before changing anything.

A tiny client plugin can log real interaction metrics while you click around:

npm install web-vitals
// app/plugins/vitals.client.ts
import { onINP, onLCP, type Metric } from 'web-vitals'

export default defineNuxtPlugin(() => {
  if (!import.meta.dev) return // dev-only logging
  const report = (metric: Metric) => {
    console.info(
      `[vitals] ${location.pathname} ${metric.name} = ${Math.round(metric.value)} ms`,
    )
  }
  onINP(report) // Interaction to Next Paint: how fast the page responds to input
  onLCP(report) // Largest Contentful Paint: how fast the main content appears
})

What this does: the .client.ts suffix makes Nuxt load the plugin only in the browser. onINP reports how long the slowest interactions took to produce a visual update, which is exactly what Vapor aims to improve. onLCP is a loading metric; use it to confirm Vapor did not make first load worse (remember the extra runtime JavaScript from Part 3).

Also record:

  • a DevTools Performance recording of the same interaction (type in search, toggle a row), noting the “Scripting” time
  • your client bundle size for the page, for example with npx nuxt analyze

Gate: numbers saved somewhere you can compare against later.

Phase 2: Start with a leaf

Convert one small, self-contained component that has no children of its own, such as a row, a card or a status pill. Leaf components are the easiest to convert and the easiest to undo.

Gate: no visual or behavioral regressions, including events (Part 8, gotcha 7) and refs (gotcha 2).

Phase 3: Convert one whole page

Now convert the hottest candidate page and the components it owns, following the boundary rule so loops live entirely inside Vapor (Part 7).

A handy trick for a fair comparison: while evaluating, keep a classic copy of the page at a second route. Since the files differ by one word, this is cheap:

app/pages/catalog.vue          ← <script setup vapor>
app/pages/catalog-classic.vue  ← same file, without vapor (temporary)

(Its children need classic copies too, otherwise the “classic” page still renders Vapor rows.) Repeat the exact interactions from Phase 1 on both routes and compare.

Gate: a measured improvement on the metric you cared about, with no loading regression you can’t accept. If there is no measurable win, roll back. Vapor that doesn’t help is just risk.

Phase 4: Expand, page by page

Repeat Phase 3 for the next candidate. Keep each page mostly in one mode. Resist converting pages that are already fast; they add pre-release risk without benefit.

Gate: each converted page shows its own win.

Phase 5: Hold or go

Until Vue 3.6 is stable, treat converted pages as an experiment you can ship to a beta audience or behind a feature branch, not as a production default. When stable 3.6 lands, re-run your measurements on it and decide.

The decision flowchart

For any single page, walk this flowchart. A “no” anywhere means “not yet”, and tells you what to fix first.

Rolling back

If a converted page misbehaves in any way:

- <script setup vapor lang="ts">
+ <script setup lang="ts">

That’s it. The component compiles back to the Virtual DOM on the next build. Nothing else in your app depended on it being Vapor. If you want to switch the whole experiment off, set vue.vapor: false as well, after removing the attributes from your components.

Part 10: Beginner FAQ, wrap-up and references

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to rewrite my templates for Vapor? No. Templates, ref, computed, watch, props, emits and slots are written the same way. The change is the vapor attribute, plus avoiding the patterns in Part 8.

Will my bundle get smaller? Not in Nuxt 4.6. Interop mode ships the Vapor runtime alongside the Virtual DOM runtime, so expect slightly more JavaScript. The bundle-size savings only apply to pure Vapor apps, which Nuxt doesn’t support yet.

Does server-side rendering still work? Yes. Vapor pages are server-rendered and then hydrated in the browser, and useAsyncData was made Vapor-aware for this. Hydration is also one of the areas still receiving fixes in each Vue 3.6 release candidate, which is another reason to test carefully.

Can app.vue or a layout be Vapor? Nuxt's internal application root is always Virtual DOM. Layouts and app.vue sit below it, but they wrap every page, so converting them puts a mode boundary around your whole app. Start with pages instead.

Will my composables and stores keep working? Composables built on Vue reactivity and provide/inject are expected to work, which is why most Nuxt composables work unchanged. Anything that calls getCurrentInstance() or uses globalProperties will not. Test your own before relying on them.

How do I know a component really compiled as Vapor? In development, getCurrentInstance() returns null inside a Vapor component (see the check in Part 5).

Should I use this in production today? Not as a default. Vue 3.6 is still a release candidate and Nuxt labels its Vapor support experimental. Experiment on a branch, measure, and decide again when Vue 3.6 is stable.

Wrapping up

Vapor Mode is the most significant change to how Vue renders since Vue 3. It compiles the same .vue files into code that updates the DOM directly, with no VNode trees and no diffing. Nuxt 4.6 makes it adoptable without a rewrite:

  • One option in nuxt.config.ts installs the interop bridge and changes nothing by itself.
  • One word in <script setup> moves a page or component to Vapor, and removing it moves it back.
  • One rule keeps it fast: put the boundary above the loop.
  • One habit keeps it safe: measure before and after, and convert only the pages that actually win.

The interop design means you don’t have to bet your app on a release candidate. You can bet one page, see the numbers, and decide. That is how big framework changes should be adopted.

corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Domingo | 8 de novembro de 2026

Em uma entrevista realizada durante o TS Summit 2026, Guilherme Celso, presidente da ABRACEO (Associação Brasileira dos Organizadores de Corridas de Rua e Esportes Outdoor), explicou o papel da entidade no cenário nacional. A ABRACEO foi criada para profissionalizar e unir o mercado de corridas no Brasil, atuando sobre três pilares principais: educacional, networking e político.

No pilar educacional, a associação promove webinars sobre temas como entrega de kits, sinalização de trilhas, novas leis e segurança, além de realizar a ABRACEO Academy. Essa iniciativa permite que organizadores de todo o país trabalhem na São Paulo City Marathon, aprendendo na prática com a estrutura de um grande evento. O pilar de networking visa conectar os organizadores, facilitando a troca de experiências e ajuda mútua. Segundo Guilherme, isso representa uma evolução em relação ao antigo modelo de “aprender errando” ou “espionando” a concorrência.

O pilar político é atualmente o maior desafio. A falta de padronização entre os municípios e a criação de leis populistas, como a que oferece inscrição gratuita para doadores de sangue sem uma contrapartida do poder público, encarecem os custos operacionais. Esse valor acaba sendo repassado para os demais corredores, aumentando o preço das inscrições.

Guilherme também contou sobre a origem da ABRACEO, que nasceu de uma conversa entre Paulo Carelli (Iguana Sports) e Marquinhos (VO2) no TS Summit de 2019, e se consolidou durante a crise da pandemia em 2020. Atualmente com quase 100 associados, a entidade busca expandir sua atuação com Summits Regionais, já realizados em Florianópolis e com edições planejadas para Salvador e Brasília. O objetivo é conectar e apoiar organizadores de todos os portes pelo país, fortalecendo o esporte como um todo.
